summary: Jesus teaches from Simon's boat, directs an overwhelming catch, and calls Simon, James, and John to ‘catch people alive.’ He touches and cleanses a man with a severe skin disease, then withdraws to pray despite spreading fame. Friends lower a paralyzed man through a roof; Jesus forgives him and heals him as visible confirmation of the Son of Man's authority. Levi leaves his tax station and hosts a great banquet for Jesus, tax collectors, and others. Complaints about table fellowship lead to the physician saying, bridegroom image, fasting question, and paired sayings about patches and wineskins.
whyItMatters: Luke links mission, cleansing, forgiveness, restored movement, vocation, and meals. Jesus's holiness is not protected by distance from need; it moves outward, creates new communities, and repeatedly collides with systems that classify people before hearing what mercy is doing.

context.author: The anonymous writer, traditionally named Luke, retelling shared call, healing, controversy, and meal traditions in his own sequence
context.audience: Theophilus and a wider Greek-reading audience, learning how authority, forgiveness, prayer, and table fellowship fit together
context.date: Commonly dated around AD 80–90; earlier dates in the 60s and later ones into the early second century are defended
context.setting: Lake of Gennesaret, towns and houses in Galilee, a roofed home, Levi's tax station, and banquet
context.literaryForm: Call narrative, healing stories, pronouncement controversies, and wisdom comparisons

outline.heading: Teaching boat, great catch, and fisher disciples
outline.note: He teaches from Simon's boat, then says let down nets; the catch fills two boats to sinking, and they leave everything and follow him

outline.heading: A man cleansed by touch; Jesus withdraws to pray
outline.note: A man with leprosy falls on his face; Jesus touches him, saying 'I want to', and the leprosy leaves; he then withdraws to pray

outline.heading: Friends, roof, forgiveness, and a paralyzed man walking
outline.note: Men lower a paralyzed man through the tiles; Jesus forgives his sins, then tells him to take up his cot and go home

outline.heading: Levi called and a banquet with tax collectors
outline.note: Jesus tells tax collector Levi 'Follow me'; Levi leaves everything, hosts a feast, and the Pharisees complain; Jesus says the sick need a physician

outline.heading: Bridegroom, fasting, patches, and wineskins
outline.note: Asked about fasting, he speaks of the bridegroom taken away, a new patch on an old garment, and new wine in old wineskins

keyVerses.text: and so also were James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. Jesus said to Simon, “Don’t be afraid. From now on you will be catching people alive.”
keyVerses.why: Luke's verb, ‘take alive,’ turns a lethal fishing metaphor toward rescue into life.

keyVerses.text: Seeing their faith, he said to him, “Man, your sins are forgiven you.”
keyVerses.why: The friends' embodied trust and Jesus's forgiveness expand the scene beyond private belief.

keyVerses.text: I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance.”
keyVerses.why: Jesus defines his social nearness as a physician-like mission toward changed life.

questions.question: What does ‘catching people alive’ mean?
questions.answer: Luke uses zōgreō, literally ‘take alive.’ The image still involves a decisive transfer, but the added ‘alive’ resists treating evangelism as conquest or killing. Simon is called from fear into a mission that rescues people for life.

questions.question: Why does Simon call himself sinful after a catch of fish?
questions.answer: The abundance discloses holy authority inside Simon's ordinary expertise, producing awe and self-recognition like prophetic call scenes. Jesus answers ‘Don’t be afraid’ and gives vocation, not humiliation. Confession becomes the beginning of discipleship rather than a reason for exclusion.

questions.question: Does ‘leprosy’ here necessarily mean modern Hansen's disease?
questions.answer: Biblical skin-disease vocabulary covers a wider range of visible conditions than the modern diagnosis. The social and ritual stakes include exclusion and priestly certification. Jesus touches before the condition is pronounced clean, on a common reading reversing the expected direction of contamination without dismissing Torah's process.

questions.question: Why does Jesus keep withdrawing when crowds need him?
questions.answer: Luke repeatedly places prayer around major decisions and public pressure. Withdrawal is not indifference; Jesus returns to teach and heal. The rhythm refuses a model of ministry in which availability to demand replaces communion, discernment, and human limits.

questions.question: Whose faith does Jesus see in the roof scene?
questions.answer: The plural ‘their’ points to the determined group carrying the man, not only to an inward state in the patient. Their faith becomes architecture opened, obstacles crossed, and a friend placed before Jesus. The story supports communal intercession without promising that one person's faith mechanically guarantees another's cure.

questions.question: Does healing prove that the man's paralysis was caused by sin?
questions.answer: Jesus forgives first and heals as a visible answer to the dispute over authority, but he never says a specific sin caused the paralysis. The scribes' question concerns who may forgive. The scene joins spiritual and bodily restoration while resisting a universal equation between disability and guilt.

questions.question: Why eat with tax collectors and sinners if repentance matters?
questions.answer: Tax collection under imperial systems invited exploitation and social stigma. Jesus's meal grants presence before moral reform is displayed, while his physician saying names repentance as the aim. Hospitality is neither endorsement of abuse nor a purity reward for people already fixed.

questions.question: Do the wineskins mean everything old is bad?
questions.answer: The comparisons say a patch from a new garment and new wine can destroy old containers; newness requires fitting forms. But Luke alone adds that someone drinking old wine says it is good, acknowledging attachment and perhaps value. Jesus is not giving a slogan for despising Israel or all tradition.

glossary.def: Another name for the Sea of Galilee and its surrounding region.
Jesus's self-designation, drawing together human identification, suffering, authority, and, on a common reading, the imagery of Daniel 7:13.
Agent collecting revenue within Roman imperial systems, often distrusted for harshness and greed.
Animal-skin container; old skins burst when new wine is put in them (5:37).
